canonical_statement: The study evaluated adherence to consensus anticoagulation recommendations for patients treated for deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism across a representative sample of hospitals.

The final analytic sample contained 270 Medicare beneficiaries treated with intravenous heparin for deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism at 21 randomly selected Pennsylvania hospitals during 1992.

population.label: Pennsylvania Medicare beneficiaries treated with intravenous heparin for DVT or pulmonary embolism in 1992

canonical_statement: Patients were identified from 1992 Pennsylvania hospitalizations with DVT or pulmonary embolism in the principal diagnosis position, with the first qualifying admission selected for each patient.

population.label: Patients with a principal diagnosis of DVT or pulmonary embolism during 1992

canonical_statement: The study excluded patients with vena cava filter placement, in-hospital death, transfer to another acute-care facility, treatment stopped within 3 days because of a decision not to treat VTE, initial thrombolytic or therapeutic subcutaneous heparin therapy, or warfarin use before admission.

population.label: Candidate VTE hospitalizations
exclusion_criteria: Therapy stopped within 3 days because VTE was not treated

canonical_statement: Hospitals were randomly selected after stratification by size, eastern versus western Pennsylvania, and urban versus rural location; up to 18 qualifying discharges were randomly selected per facility with a target of 15 eligible discharges.

Chart abstractors confirmed that the attending physician treated the patient for DVT or pulmonary embolism, but laboratory confirmation of the VTE diagnosis was not required because the study focused on treatment practice.

Abstractors recorded the initial heparin dose, heparin duration, timing and results of the first six PTT tests in the first 72 hours, up to seven platelet counts after heparin initiation, warfarin start date, and the PT ratio or INR closest to heparin discontinuation.
Therapeutic anticoagulation was defined as the first of two consecutive PTT values greater than 1.5 times control, excluding PTTs obtained within 3 hours of the initial heparin bolus.

concept.text: Time to therapeutic PTT

outcome.definition: First of two consecutive PTTs >1.5 times control; PTTs within 3 h of initial bolus excluded

canonical_statement: Platelet-monitoring adherence was assessed by whether at least one platelet count was obtained during the first 3 days and during the first 7 days after heparin initiation.

concept.text: Platelet count monitoring during heparin therapy

outcome.definition: At least one platelet count within 3 days and within 7 days of heparin initiation

canonical_statement: Adequate heparin duration was defined as at least 120 hours (5 days) of intravenous heparin therapy, without requiring the PTT to remain therapeutic throughout that interval.

concept.text: Heparin treatment duration at least 5 days

outcome.definition: At least 120 hours of IV heparin; therapeutic PTT not required throughout

canonical_statement: Heparin-warfarin overlap was considered adequate when heparin was continued until the PT ratio was at least 1.3 or the INR was at least 2.0.

concept.text: Heparin continued until therapeutic warfarin anticoagulation

outcome.definition: PT ratio >=1.3 or INR >=2.0 before heparin discontinuation

canonical_statement: Population estimates and confidence intervals were calculated with generalized estimating equations to account for clustering of patients within hospitals; time to therapeutic PTT used survival analysis, and length of stay was log-transformed before comparison.
A 5,000-unit heparin bolus was used to start therapy in 172 patients (64%).

canonical_statement: The authors noted that achieving a therapeutic PTT within 24 hours was not supported by a randomized controlled trial and was based on retrospective comparisons, with some investigators questioning its validity as a recurrence-risk target.
The study used 1.5 times control as the lower therapeutic PTT threshold even though the authors acknowledged that the true therapeutic range varies by reagent lot and laboratory.

The authors concluded that compliance with consensus anticoagulation recommendations was fair but variable across hospitals and that simple interventions could potentially improve care and reduce costs.

The authors suggested that heparin dosing nomograms were a plausible way to improve timely therapeutic anticoagulation because hospitals using nomograms in prior studies achieved higher rates than those observed here.

The analyses were performed under Health Care Financing Administration contract 500-96-P708 as part of the Health Care Quality Improvement Program; the authors stated that the work required no special funding beyond the contractor program.
